ut_little_cottonwood_canyon.blurb: A steep glacial canyon in the Central Wasatch, roughly twenty minutes from Salt Lake City, with granite-like quartz monzonite walls rising beside the road and a river below. Bouldering is the biggest part of the picture, with problems at every level from V0 up to very hard, and trad comes next, with a good number of sport routes too. Free climbing mostly runs from the 5.8 range to 5.12, with moderates well covered, plus a little ice, aid and alpine. Expect crystalline holds, plenty of friction and abrasive skin wear. Fall is the sweet spot, spring depends on snowmelt, and the shadier south side or the high boulders around White Pine help in summer. Gate Buttress, Hellgate Cliffs, Albion Basin and the boulder fields are the main hubs.

ut_central_utah.blurb: A loose grouping of small canyons and valleys in the middle of the state, reached from the Nephi side off the interstate or from Price along the highway. Two hubs carry most of the climbing. Maple Canyon is the sport destination, where walls are packed with embedded cobblestones and routes run from short pitches to tall cliffs, with shade that keeps summer days bearable. Joe's Valley is the bouldering hub, on smooth sandstone with flat landings. Sport and bouldering dominate, with a wide spread from easy problems to hard ones, and sport mostly in the 5.9 to 5.13 range. Triassic, Nephi, Huntington Canyon and Price Canyon add quieter walls, and Huntington Canyon also offers winter ice.

ut_saint_george.blurb: The sunny desert hub of southwest Utah, popular as a cold-season escape thanks to mild winters. Sport climbing is the largest share, bouldering is nearly as big, and there is a smaller helping of trad and top-rope. Sport routes cluster in the 5.9 to 5.12 range, with some easier and harder lines, while boulder problems stretch from V0 to the double digits with plenty of V2 to V5. Rock varies by crag: Black Rocks is a basalt canyon, Moe's Valley and Green Valley Gap are sandstone, and limestone shows up near Hurricane. Moe's Valley, Utah Hills, Garth Rocks, Crawdad Canyon and Cottonwood Springs are among the larger bases. Winter, spring and fall suit most walls, and summer heat pushes climbers toward shade. Sandstone should be left alone after rain.

co_nine_mile_bouldering.blurb: A huge boulder field draped along the highway as it climbs from the Gunnison River toward the top of the Uncompahgre Plateau, in Unaweep Canyon country near Grand Junction. This is bouldering only, and mostly friendly: V1 to V4 make up the bulk, with a solid base of easier warm-ups and a thinner tail of hard problems up to the V10s. The sandstone changes within a few feet, from crumbly coarse layers to tougher iron-rich skin, and only a fraction of the blocks are worth climbing, though thousands exist. Mecca, Blue Moon, Pool of Plenty, Black Wave and Reba are among the larger sectors. Approaches are short and crowds are thin. Spring and fall are comfortable, shaded blocks help in summer, and crisp winter days can bring good friction.

ca_high_desert.blurb: A scattered stretch of the Mojave north and east of the San Bernardino Mountains, centered on Apple Valley and Barstow, with outliers toward Lucerne Valley, Landers, Johnson Valley and Victorville. Sport climbing leads, with bouldering second and a modest amount of trad and top-rope. Sport routes are mostly 5.8 to 5.11, with some 5.12, so the range suits intermediates best, and boulder problems run heavily toward the easy end. The terrain is open and exposed with little shade, and single-pitch sport walls of roughly seventy to a hundred feet are typical. Rock quality varies widely, from firm sandstone at some crags to loose, chossy boulders at others, so helmets and extra pads are wise. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons, and summer afternoons turn dangerously hot.

ca_i_80_corridor.blurb: The climbing that lines the interstate from the Sierra foothills near Auburn up over Donner Summit toward Truckee. Bouldering makes up about half of the climbs, followed by sport and then trad, with a sprinkling of mixed lines and top-ropes. Most free routes fall between 5.7 and 5.12, with the 5.10 to 5.11 band thickest. Rock changes along the way. Donner Summit and the Emeralds are granite, Auburn's quarry crags are limestone, and Big Chief is volcanic. Donner Summit is the headline stop, with trad, multi-pitch, sport and steep boulders above the lake. Bowman and the Emeralds hold concentrated sport, and Rainbow and Rocklin offer boulders. Summer is prime up high, while the foothill walls suit fall through spring and the south-facing ones stay usable in winter.
